title: Transport was Tunisia's largest final-energy consumer in 2024, with petroleum products supplying about 90%

rootCauses.cause: Transport energy use is concentrated in road transport, and the transport balance is dominated by petroleum products; the available balance describes this structure but does not establish its underlying behavioural, economic or policy causes.

dataGaps: ONEM's 2024 report gives transport as 35% of final demand in its narrative and sector summary table when biomass is included, but gives 37% in the same table excluding biomass. The report text also says the transport share rises to 37% excluding biomass. Because 37% is denominator-specific, the finding uses the 35% with-biomass value; no unresolved conflict remains in the denominator-labelled published figures.
Not independently reopened: the ANME transport profile figures (undated 36% share, road 90%, more than 55% of petroleum-product use) (SRC-TG-313).
No current fleet fuel-efficiency series or recent transport-mode split was verified; this finding does not estimate avoidable fuel imports.
The national balance and sector profile describe the end-use mix, not causal drivers such as passenger versus freight activity, fleet age, travel demand or modal policy.
author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: ONEM's 2024 national energy balance records 2,721 ktep of final energy consumption by transport, the largest sector. The report narrative gives its share as 35%; Table 6 reports 35% with biomass included and 37% without…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
ONEM's 2024 national energy balance records 2,721 ktep of final energy consumption by transport, the largest sector. The report narrative gives its share as 35%; Table 6 reports 35% with biomass included and 37% without biomass, and the accompanying text explicitly says the share rises to 37% when biomass is excluded. The percentage differs by denominator, not because of a second transport total (SRC-TG-222).

In the detailed 2024 balance, petroleum products total 2,437 ktep of transport's 2,721 ktep, or 89.6% (calculated from the source values). The road row is 2,423 ktep, or 89.0% of transport consumption (also calculated from source values). These are distinct indicators: petroleum is an energy-carrier subtotal, while road is an end-use sub-sector. The table also shows non-petroleum inputs, so petroleum is dominant rather than exclusive (SRC-TG-222).

ANME's transport profile independently describes transport as the largest energy-consuming sector and gives an undated 36% share, with road at 90% of transport use and transport responsible for more than 55% of national petroleum-product use. Because the page does not date those figures and its aggregate wording does not resolve ONEM's internal 2024 discrepancy, it is used only as a separate, undated corroboration of the broad sector pattern (SRC-TG-313). ONEM reports that transport final consumption rose 4% in 2024 compared with 2023; this is a single-year change, so no multi-year trend is claimed (SRC-TG-222). The finding links transport activity to liquid-fuel demand without repeating the national import-bill issue in FND-TG-131.

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content: The balance establishes concentration in road transport and petroleum products, not why that pattern exists. It does not separate passenger and freight demand, fleet age or efficiency, travel demand, or the effects of transport policy. The structural description is therefore not presented as a demonstrated causal explanation.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content: The dated primary evidence is ONEM's official 2024 national energy balance and accompanying report (SRC-TG-222). It directly reports the 2,721 ktep transport total, 2,437 ktep petroleum subtotal and 2,423 ktep road row; the 89.6% and 89.0% ratios are arithmetic derived from those reported values. The report presents the 35% share including biomass and the 37% share excluding biomass. ANME's undated profile (SRC-TG-313) offers secondary corroboration, not a replacement dated series. The World Bank's 2022 fuel-supply context in SRC-TG-311 is not used to infer 2024 imports. The national energy-management strategy (SRC-TG-290) is retained as context for the phase-2 lead, not as evidence for the 2024 indicators.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: High for the official 2024 transport total, its first-place ranking, and the two calculated composition ratios. ONEM's 35% share includes biomass; its 37% share excludes biomass. No causal claim is made about why road transport dominates.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content: Fuel use connects transport to refining and imported petroleum supply. This finding describes end use and does not quantify the import-bill effect.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content: - Transport efficiency actions described in the national energy-management strategy (SRC-TG-290).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
ONEM’s 2024 balance records 2,721 ktoe consumed by transport, including 2,437 ktoe of petroleum products. ANME independently identifies transport as the largest sector, without dating its percentage; use ONEM for the 2024 share (SRC-TG-312, SRC-TG-313).

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked ONEM Rapport Bilan Énergétique 2024 (SRC-TG-222): Tableau 6 (printed p. 18, transport 2,721 ktep, 35% with biomass and 37% without), section 1.4 (p. 17, transport the first consuming sector), the national balance (petroleum products 2,437 ktep; road 2,423 ktep), Figures 12 and 13 (p. 20, printed 89.1% road and 89.5% petroleum products) and the transport text (p. 20, +4% against 2023, 89% road, about 90% petroleum products). Corrections: the calculated shares now note the percentages ONEM prints (89.5% and 89.1%); the trend field is set to unknown because the previous "worsening" rested on a single year (+4% in 2024, now stated as such). The ANME corroboration was not reopened and is listed in data_gaps. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

resolvedSources.title: Evolution du bilan énergétique au cours de la période 2010-2024 (Rapport bilan énergétique 2024)
resolvedSources.publisher: Observatoire National de l'Energie et des Mines (ONEM), Ministère de l'Industrie, des Mines et de l'Energie
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF p. 37-38, section 2.2.4 "Pertes électriques dans le réseau":

> Cet indicateur renseigne sur le niveau de performance du système de distribution et de transport d'électricité. [...] Il est défini comme le rapport entre les pertes d'électricité dans le réseau et la production brute d'électricité. [...] Il traduit alors le taux de pertes à la fois technique et commerciale.

English gloss: the loss rate is network electricity losses divided by gross electricity
production. It covers both technical and commercial losses.

PDF p. 38, Figure 33 "Evolution de taux de perte du système de distribution et de transmission d'électricité". Data labels read from the rendered page image:

> 2010 11,4% | 2011 13,7% | 2012 15,2% | 2013 14,7% | 2014 14,8% | 2015 16,1% | 2016 15,8% | 2017 17,4% | 2018 17,1% | 2019 16,6% | 2020 17,4% | 2021 21,1% | 2022 21,7% | 2023 20,0% | 2024 21,1%

English gloss: total loss rate by year, 2010-2024.

PDF p. 38, text under the figure:

> D'après le graphique ci-dessus, nous remarquons que le taux de pertes a augmenté, entre 2010 et 2024, passant de 11.4% à 21.1%. Sur l'ensemble de la période 2010-2024, cet indicateur aurait augmenté de plus de 10 points : Les pertes de transport n'ont pas dépassé les 2.23% en 2024 [note 18], celles relatives à la distribution se situent dans la fourchette de 7-9%. La plus grande partie des pertes provient de détournement d'électricité, un phénomène qui ne cesse d'augmenter malgré qu'une amende de 2000 dinars est prévue par la Loi [note 19] pour chaque opération de ce genre.

> 18 Rapport annuel d'activité de la STEG de l'année 2024.
> 19 Selon le décret gouvernemental n° 2018-59 du 16 janvier 2018, publié dans le JORT du 19 janvier 2018.

English gloss: the loss rate rose from 11.4% (2010) to 21.1% (2024), more than 10 points.
Transmission losses did not exceed 2.23% in 2024 and distribution losses are in the 7-9% range
(both citing STEG's 2024 annual activity report). Most losses come from electricity theft, which
keeps growing even though the rules set a fine of 2,000 dinars for each case (Government Decree
2018-59 of 16 January 2018).

p. 17, section 1.4 (added for FND-TG-290/291):

> En 2024 et avec 2,7 Mtep, le secteur du transport est le premier secteur consommateur d'énergie ; soit 35% de la consommation finale nationale. Le secteur de l'industrie suit, avec 25% de la demande finale, en avance devant le secteur résidentiel (23%).

English gloss: in 2024 transport is the largest final consumer (35%), industry second (25%),
ahead of residential (23%).

p. 18, Tableau 6 and "Secteur industriel":

> Industrie | 1 914 | 25% (avec biomasse) | 1 902 | 26% (sans biomasse)

> En 2024, la consommation d'énergie dans le secteur industriel est dominée par le gaz naturel (40%) et les produits pétroliers (34%). L'électricité représente cependant une part non négligeable avec plus de 25%. Par rapport à 2023, la consommation d'énergie finale dans l'industrie a enregistré une baisse remarquable de 4%. Entre 2023 et 2024, la part de gaz naturel a augmenté en faveur de celle des produits pétroliers qui est passée de 37% à 34% suite notamment à la substitution partielle du gaz naturel par le petcoke chez certaines cimenteries.

English gloss: industrial final consumption was 1,914 ktep in 2024 (25% of final demand), -4% on
2023; gas 40%, petroleum products 34%, electricity over 25%. The text says the gas share rose
while petroleum products fell from 37% to 34%, but attributes this to "partial substitution of
natural gas by petcoke"; the direction of that sentence is reversed relative to the numbers
(the 2023 report used the same wording for a rise in petroleum products). See Notes.

p. 19, text, Figure 10 and Figure 11:

> L'Utilisation des combustibles alternatifs par le secteur industriel a commencé depuis 2011 chez certaines cimenteries, il s'agit plus précisément du grignon d'olive. [...] sa part a augmenté passant de 0.1% en 2023 à 0.6% en 2024.

> Figure 10: 2023: 1994 Ktep (Produits pétroliers 37,3% | Gaz naturel 38,0% | Electricité 24,5% | Biomasse 0,1%) ; 2024: 1914 ktep (Produits pétroliers 34,1% | Gaz naturel 40,2% | Electricité 25,1% | Biomasse 0,6%) ; - 4%

> Le pet coke est le principal produit pétrolier utilisé dans l'industrie et plus précisément dans les cimenteries, il représente 72% du total produits pétroliers suivi par le fuel lourd avec 16% du total.

English gloss: some cement plants have used olive pomace as alternative fuel since 2011 (0.6% of
industrial energy in 2024). Industrial consumption fell from 1,994 ktep (2023) to 1,914 ktep
(2024). Petcoke, used mainly in cement plants, is 72% of the petroleum products used by industry.

p. 26, text:

> L'industrie enregistre une baisse de 4 %, reflétant un léger ralentissement de l'activité ou des gains d'efficacité.

English gloss: industry's 4% fall (2023-2024) reflects either a slight slowdown in activity or
efficiency gains; ONEM does not say which.

p. 40, "Tableau récapitulatif des Indicateurs clés", row "Dont industrie" (share of final energy consumption):

> 2010: 28% | 2011: 27% | 2012: 29% | 2013: 29% | 2014: 30% | 2015: 29% | 2016: 28% | 2017: 27% | 2018: 27% | 2019: 26% | 2020: 25% | 2021: 25% | 2022: 25% | 2023: 24% | 2024: 25%

p. 43, annex "Bilan national de l'énergie 2024" (ktep), rows "Industrie", "Produits minéraux non métalliques", "Chimie"; columns Total, Total produits pétroliers, GPL, Gasoil, Fuel oil, PETCOKE, Gaz naturel, renouvelables/biomasse, Electricité:

> Industrie | 1 914 | 653 | 27 | 49 | 104 | 473 | 769 | 11,5 | 480
> Chimie | 174 | — | — | — | — | — | 99 | — | 74
> Produits minéraux non métalliques | 959 | 473 | — | — | — | 473 | 362 | 11 | 113

p. 42, annex "Bilan national de l'énergie 2023", same rows:

> Industrie | 1 994 | 744 | 30 | 50 | 132 | 532 | 758 | 2,9 | 489
> Chimie | 149 | — | — | — | — | — | 80 | — | 70
> Produits minéraux non métalliques | 1 054 | 532 | — | — | — | 532 | 402 | 3 | 118

English gloss: in 2024 the non-metallic minerals branch (cement, lime, bricks, ceramics, glass)
used 959 of industry's 1,914 ktep (50%), including all 473 ktep of industrial petcoke. Chemicals
used 174 ktep. In 2023 the branch used 1,054 of 1,994 ktep, with 532 ktep of petcoke.
resolvedSources.notes:
The chart's year-to-value mapping was checked against the rendered page image (PyMuPDF, 110
dpi), because the text layer scrambles the label order. The report gives no figure for theft
itself. "Most losses" from theft is the report's own reading of what is left after technical
losses. Read literally, technical losses are 2.23% + 7-9%, so about 9-11% of 21.1%. That
residual is derived by us and is not stated in the source. The denominator is gross production,
so the rate is not directly comparable with utility figures that use net generation or energy
injected into the grid.

Note added for FND-TG-290: the p. 19 text layer contains a stray "2121 ktep" label that is not
shown on the rendered page; the rendered Figure 10 reads 1,994 ktep (2023) and 1,914 ktep (2024),
matching the annex. The p. 18 sentence on gas/petcoke substitution reads reversed against its own
numbers (petroleum share falling); use the annex petcoke column (532 to 473 ktep) instead. The
annex rows on pp. 42-43 were rebuilt from word positions in the text layer; the branch rows add
up (959 = 473 + 362 + 11 + 113).

resolvedSources.title: Stratégie nationale de maîtrise de l'énergie, objectifs, moyens et enjeux (synthèse, juin 2014)
resolvedSources.publisher: Ministère de l'Industrie, de l'Energie et des Mines (DGE) and Agence Nationale pour la Maîtrise de l'Energie (ANME); published by GIZ
resolvedSources.extracts:
p. 17, section 3.1 "Le renforcement de la maîtrise de la demande d'énergie":

> La Loi de maîtrise de l'énergie promulguée le 2 Août 2004 et le Fonds National de Maîtrise de l'Energie (FNME), devenu le Fonds de Transition Energétique (FTE) créé en 2005 ont constitué les deux fers de lance pour dynamiser le soutien des investissements en matière d'utilisation rationnelle de l'énergie. Les principales actions ayant généré des économies d'énergie significatives sont les contrats programme, la diffusion des lampes à basse consommation, la cogénération et la certification des réfrigérateurs.

> Sur la période 2000-2012, les programmes de maîtrise de la demande d'énergie lancés par l'ANME ont permis une baisse de l'intensité énergétique primaire de 2% par an (figure 3).

English gloss: the energy management law of 2 August 2004 and the efficiency fund created in
2005 drove investment in rational energy use; programme contracts, efficient lamps, cogeneration
and fridge labelling produced the main savings. Over 2000-2012, ANME's demand-side programmes
brought primary energy intensity down by 2% a year.

p. 18, "Le plan d'action par secteur":

> Il s'agit de mobiliser activement le gisement d'économie d'énergie dans trois grands secteurs : l'industrie, les bâtiments et les transports, représentant respectivement 51%, 26% et 25% des économies d'énergie réalisées sur la consommation énergétique finale prévues par le plan d'action.

English gloss: industry was to provide 51% of the final-energy savings planned in the 2014-2020
action plan (buildings 26%, transport 25%, as printed).

p. 19, "Cogénération":

> Impulsion du développement de la cogénération dans les secteurs de l'industrie et du tertiaire. L'objectif est d'atteindre une capacité de 440 MW en 2020.

English gloss: the cogeneration target was 440 MW in industry and tertiary by 2020.

p. 33, "Les textes régissant les obligations de consommateurs d'énergie":

> Revoir les conditions d'application de l'audit énergétique (seuil, fréquence, etc.).

> Introduire progressivement les obligations de monitoring et d'évaluation des actions d'économie d'énergie subventionnées par le FTE au niveau des établissements assujettis à l'obligation de l'audit énergétique.

English gloss: the strategy recommended revising how the mandatory energy audit applies
(threshold, frequency) and gradually introducing monitoring and evaluation obligations for
FTE-subsidised savings actions in establishments subject to the audit.
resolvedSources.notes:
Government strategy synthesis, prepared with German cooperation. The 2% a year figure for
2000-2012 is the authors' own assessment of their programmes and uses a 1990-price GDP series;
it is not directly comparable to ONEM's 2010-2019 series (SRC-TG-130). The sector shares on p. 18
sum to 102% as printed.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Economic Monitor, Spring 2023: Reforming Energy Subsidies for a More Sustainable Tunisia
resolvedSources.extracts:
Part A, section 3, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 26):

> At the end of 2021, the Tunisian Company of Electricity and Gas (STEG) in charge of importing gas for electricity production and the Tunisian Company of Refining Industry (STIR) in charge of importing gasoline, had accumulated 7.9 billion dinars of debts with foreign banks and 4.3 billion dinars of debts with suppliers. However, strategy appears to have reached its limits as their rising debt constrains SOEs' ability to increase further their indebtedness.

> With dwindling reserves and increasing SOE debt, the rising CAD has translated in sustained shortages of basic products. This context has made it difficult to secure sufficient foreign exchange to cover the rising import bill. As a result, the economy experienced sustained shortages of many basic products since March 2022, including fuels (October 2022), cereals (March 2022), sugar, dairy products (November 2022), coffee (January 2023) and pharmaceutical products.

> As a result, reserves declined to TND 22 billion TND covering 95 days of imports by mid-February 2023, from TND 23.4 billion, covering 133 days of imports in January 2022.

Part B, printed p. 15 (PDF p. 35):

> In the case of fuels (diesel and petrol), the subsidy is absorbed by the state-owned enterprise (SOE) STIR (Société Tunisienne des Industries de Raffinage), which holds the monopoly of import (of crude and refined oil), refining and wholesale markets. About 90 percent of Tunisia's needs are satisfied directly or indirectly from international markets, where STIR sources these products at international market prices.

Footnote 4, same page:

> 68 percent of fuel consumed in Tunisia in 2022 was imported directly, 22 percent was imported as crude oil and then refined domestically by STIR, and 10 percent was produced (by ETAP) and refined (by STIR) domestically.

English gloss: at end-2021 STEG and STIR together owed TND 7.9 billion to foreign banks and TND
4.3 billion to suppliers, and their debt limited further borrowing. Foreign-exchange constraints
led to shortages of many basic products from March 2022, including fuels from October 2022. STIR
holds the import, refining and wholesale monopoly and absorbs the fuel subsidy; about 90% of needs
are met directly or indirectly from international markets. In 2022,
68% of fuel consumed was imported as product, 22% was refined from imported crude and 10% was
refined from domestic crude.
resolvedSources.notes:
Text extracted with pdftotext; the page layout is two-column, so sentences were reassembled in
reading order. The 22% + 10% share refined by
STIR in 2022 matches ONEM's 2022 STIR coverage rate of 32% (all production, SRC-TG-220). The
STEG and STIR debt figures are combined; the report does not split them. The report does not
quantify how long or how severe the October 2022 fuel shortages were.
